topic.title: Incident Response and Recovery — operate AI systems safely under failure

outcomes: Classify AI incidents by user impact, security/privacy exposure, scope, persistence and recoverability.
Run a structured incident lifecycle from detection and triage through containment, eradication, recovery and blameless review.
Select safe containment actions for prompt injection, tenant isolation breaches, compromised artifacts, unsafe tools, provider outages and runaway cost.
Preserve trustworthy, privacy-aware evidence with timestamps, immutable identifiers, digests, access controls and chain-of-custody records.
Restore from a known-good immutable release, rotate credentials, validate data integrity and use staged recovery with SLO/quality guardrails.
Write actionable postmortems and run deterministic tabletop/failure-injection exercises with owners, deadlines and verification evidence.
prerequisites: Stage 10 Topics 4–5 supply chain and tracing
Stage 10 Topics 6–7 SLOs, reliability and cost controls
Basic deployment rollback, access control and operational monitoring

glossary.definition: An unplanned event that causes or threatens user impact, security/privacy harm, data integrity loss, policy violation or service degradation.
A priority classification based on impact, scope, urgency and risk, not the seniority of the reporter.
The person coordinating response priorities, roles, decisions and communication during an incident.
Actions that limit ongoing harm or blast radius while preserving enough evidence to investigate.
Removal of the underlying cause, such as a compromised credential, poisoned artifact or unsafe configuration.
Restoring service using verified known-good components and monitoring for recurrence.
A record of who collected, accessed, transferred or transformed evidence and when.
A factual review focused on system conditions, contributing factors and corrective actions rather than individual blame.
A set of explicit security, quality, data-integrity and reliability checks that must pass before normal traffic resumes.

explanation.problem: AI incidents can affect more than uptime. A prompt-injection exploit may exfiltrate data through tools; a tenant isolation bug may expose another customer's documents; a compromised model artifact may change deployed behavior; an unsafe tool call may mutate production data; and runaway retries can create a denial-of-wallet event. Recovery without a disciplined process can destroy evidence or reintroduce the same failure.
explanation.plainLanguage:
Treat an incident as a coordinated response, not an improvised debugging session. First establish what is happening, who is affected, whether harm is continuing and who is leading the response. Assign an incident commander, an operations lead, a security/privacy lead and a communications owner when the impact warrants it. Keep one timeline and one source of truth for decisions.

Severity should reflect user impact, data exposure, security risk, scope and urgency. A confirmed cross-tenant data disclosure or active credential compromise may be the highest severity even if the service is still responding. A short regional provider outage with a safe fallback may be lower severity. Define severity levels and escalation targets before an incident; do not improvise them during an outage.

Containment reduces ongoing harm. For a suspected credential leak, revoke and rotate the credential, disable affected integrations and inspect access logs. For a tenant isolation breach, block the affected data path, disable unsafe cache/retrieval paths, revoke exposed links and preserve a list of affected resources. For a compromised model or package, quarantine the artifact and stop promotion. For unsafe tool execution, disable the tool capability or require human approval. For provider failure, open the circuit breaker and shift to an explicitly safe degraded mode. For runaway cost, cap or suspend the expensive workflow and enforce tenant budgets.

Preserve evidence before destructive cleanup where possible. Capture incident IDs, timestamps, trace IDs, deployment and model digests, configuration versions, relevant redacted logs, access decisions, queue identifiers and artifact provenance. Record who collected the evidence and its digest. Avoid copying raw prompts, customer documents, tokens or secrets into broad incident channels. Restrict evidence access, preserve original copies and document any redaction or transformation. If credentials may be exposed, rotate them; do not keep a secret alive solely for forensic convenience.

Eradicate the root cause and recover from a known-good state. Roll back to an immutable release digest, restore trusted model/data artifacts, reprocess only validated data, rebuild caches and vector indexes with tenant/ACL checks, and verify credentials and permissions. Do not simply restart a compromised service. Recovery gates should include security regression tests, data integrity, model quality/safety evaluation, tenant isolation, SLO health, cost guardrails and operational monitoring. Use a canary or staged rollout before full traffic resumes.

After recovery, write a blameless postmortem. Include impact, detection, timeline, containment, root and contributing causes, what went well, what made response harder, and corrective actions. Every action needs an owner, due date, priority and verification method. Distinguish immediate fixes from systemic improvements such as better telemetry, safer defaults, isolation tests, release attestations, runbooks or alert tuning.

Practice before the real incident. Run tabletop exercises for cross-tenant exposure, compromised model artifacts, prompt injection with tool access, provider outage, queue backlog and denial-of-wallet. Inject failures in a controlled environment, test escalation and communications, and measure time to detect, contain and recover. A runbook that has never been exercised is only a hypothesis.
explanation.mentalModel: Detect → declare and classify → assign commander/roles → contain blast radius → preserve privacy-aware evidence → eradicate cause → recover from known-good state → validate security/quality/SLO gates → communicate and learn.
limitations: Severity examples are starting points; organizations must define legal, regulatory, contractual and customer-notification obligations with qualified owners.
Evidence preservation must not delay urgent containment of active harm or credential compromise.
A simulator demonstrates response logic but cannot determine real breach scope, legal notification duties or forensic attribution.
Rollback does not automatically restore data integrity, revoke leaked credentials or invalidate cached/signed URLs.
AI quality incidents can be statistically subtle; recovery requires representative evaluation data and ongoing monitoring, not only a service health check.
Postmortems should be blameless but still assign clear ownership and deadlines for corrective actions.
explanation.everydayAnalogy: When a building alarm sounds, the team first protects people and limits danger, then records what happened, removes the hazard, checks the building before reopening and reviews how to prevent recurrence. Restarting the lights is not the same as proving the building is safe.
explanation.mathMadeSimple: Track three operational durations: time to detect (TTD), time to contain (TTC) and time to recover (TTR). If an incident begins at 09:00, is detected at 09:12, contained at 09:30 and service is safely restored at 10:15, TTD=12 minutes, TTC=18 minutes after detection, and TTR=45 minutes after containment (75 minutes from incident start). These metrics help improve systems, not rank individuals.
explanation.productionImpact: Prepare severity definitions, incident roles and category-specific runbooks; contain active harm quickly; preserve redacted verifiable evidence; restore only known-good immutable releases; validate security, data, quality, SLO and cost gates; and turn each incident into owned, testable corrective actions.

useCase.scenario: A production RAG-agent service receives an alert that a tool integration may have exposed one tenant's document references to another tenant. The service is partially available, logs contain sensitive metadata, a background indexing queue is running and a recent model release changed retrieval behavior. Respond without destroying evidence or reopening the exposure during recovery.
inputs: Alert, severity indicators and affected time window
Trace IDs, request IDs, deployment/model digests and config versions
Redacted access logs, audit decisions and queue metadata
Current rollback target and known-good artifact attestations
Security, quality, SLO and data-integrity recovery checks
constraints: Stop active exposure before investigating nonessential details.
Do not publish raw prompts, documents, credentials or tenant secrets in broad channels.
Preserve evidence with collection time, source, digest, access history and transformation notes.
Do not use a mutable tag as a rollback target; use a verified immutable release digest.
Recovery requires tenant isolation, cache/vector/object, credential and queue checks.
Do not claim a tool action or customer notification occurred unless verified.
Every postmortem action has an owner, due date and evidence of completion.
outputs: Evidence manifest with redaction and custody metadata
Known-good recovery plan and verification results
useCase.successMetric: Exposure is contained quickly, evidence remains trustworthy and privacy-aware, service is restored from a verified release only after recovery gates pass, and corrective actions are owned and tested.

components: Privacy-aware evidence vault and custody log

trustBoundaries: Incident channels and tickets are not automatically approved locations for customer content or secrets.
Evidence access is role-based and audited; redaction is recorded without overwriting originals where retention permits.
Containment actions are scoped and approved according to incident authority; destructive actions require extra care unless active harm requires immediate response.
Rollback artifacts and model versions must be verified against trusted digests and provenance.
Customer/legal/regulatory communication is handled by authorized owners with verified facts.
failurePaths: Unclear ownership: declare an incident commander and record roles before parallel actions begin.
Active data exfiltration: disable the affected path, revoke links/credentials and stop further access while preserving minimal evidence.
Artifact compromise: quarantine the digest, stop rollout and restore a known-good signed artifact.
Evidence contains secrets: restrict access, redact derived copies, rotate exposed credentials and preserve custody metadata.
Rollback reintroduces old vulnerability: run recovery gates and regression tests before staged traffic.
Queue replays harmful jobs: pause consumers, preserve queue metadata, deduplicate and revalidate before resuming.
Postmortem actions lack owners: block closure until owner, due date and verification criteria are recorded.

steps.label: Detect and declare
steps.explanation: Correlate alerts, open an incident record and appoint an incident commander.
steps.expectedState: One timeline and clear response ownership.

steps.label: Classify severity
steps.explanation: Assess user impact, security/privacy exposure, scope and urgency.
steps.expectedState: Severity and escalation path are explicit.

steps.label: Contain active harm
steps.explanation: Disable the affected capability, revoke credentials or stop unsafe traffic using the narrowest effective control.

accessibility: Every stage names the action, decision and expected state in text; severity levels and containment outcomes are not represented by color alone.
A static lifecycle diagram and step-by-step controls support reduced-motion and keyboard navigation.

stages.title: Detect and declare
stages.narration: An alert indicates possible cross-tenant document access; create an incident and appoint a commander.
stages.transformation: Correlate alert, deployment and affected time window.

stages.title: Classify impact
stages.narration: Assess whether data was exposed, how many tenants/resources are affected and whether access continues.
stages.transformation: Apply the severity matrix and escalation policy.

stages.title: Contain
stages.narration: Disable the unsafe retrieval/tool path, revoke exposed links and pause affected consumers.
stages.transformation: Stop active access while preserving necessary queue and audit metadata.

stages.title: Preserve evidence
stages.narration: Store redacted logs, trace IDs, release digests and collection metadata in a restricted evidence vault.
stages.input: Logs, traces, artifact and config references
stages.transformation: Hash evidence and record collector, timestamp and transformations.

stages.title: Recover safely
stages.narration: Restore a known-good immutable release only after isolation, cache, vector, object and credential checks pass.
stages.transformation: Run security regression, data integrity, quality and SLO gates; canary traffic.

stages.title: Learn and prevent
stages.narration: Publish a blameless timeline and assign measurable corrective actions.
stages.transformation: Create actions with owners, due dates and verification tests.

controls.name: incident_category
controls.effect: Select tenant exposure, artifact compromise, provider outage, unsafe tool action or cost runaway to load category-specific containment steps.

controls.name: active_harm
controls.effect: Toggle whether harm is ongoing; active harm requires containment before extended investigation.

controls.name: recovery_gates
controls.effect: Toggle whether all security/data/quality/SLO gates pass; recovery cannot complete until required gates pass.

animation.accessibilitySummary: Six narrated stages expose decision inputs, actions and expected outputs. Active-harm, severity and recovery-gate states are explicitly labeled in text.

workedExample.problem: At 09:12, security monitoring detects possible cross-tenant document access caused by a recently deployed RAG retrieval adapter. The service remains partially available; indexing workers continue to run; traces and logs contain sensitive metadata.
workedExample.input: Incident begins at 09:00; alert at 09:12; containment at 09:30; safe recovery at 10:15. Suspected affected resource IDs and trace IDs are available; raw prompts and access tokens must not be copied into broad channels.

steps.reasoning: Create one incident record, appoint a commander and security/privacy lead, define affected time window and identify possible tenant exposure.
steps.result: High-severity security incident with explicit owner and timeline.

steps.reasoning: Disable the affected retrieval/tool capability, pause relevant index consumers and revoke exposed object links while retaining queue metadata.
steps.result: New cross-tenant access is blocked; user impact is documented.

steps.reasoning: Collect redacted access decisions, trace IDs, release/config digests and affected resource references; hash evidence and record collector/time/access.
steps.result: Restricted evidence manifest with custody metadata and no raw secrets in incident channels.

steps.reasoning: Fix tenant predicate and cache/vector/object ownership checks, rotate any exposed credentials and invalidate unsafe cached entries.
steps.result: Root cause removed and regression tests added.

steps.reasoning: Run cross-tenant negative tests, cache/vector/object checks, queue replay review, data integrity, model quality and SLO gates.
steps.result: Recovery is blocked until every required gate passes.

steps.reasoning: Deploy the known-good immutable digest via canary, monitor for recurrence and publish a blameless postmortem with owners and due dates.
steps.result: Safe recovery at 10:15; TTD=12 minutes, TTC=18 minutes and recovery after containment=45 minutes.

workedExample.expectedOutput: The incident is contained by 09:30, evidence is preserved with privacy controls, the root cause is eradicated, and traffic is restored at 10:15 only after security and reliability gates pass. A postmortem assigns verified corrective actions.

implementations.expectedResult: Offline incident simulator classifies severity, selects category-specific containment, validates lifecycle transitions, hashes redacted evidence and checks recovery/postmortem gates.
Production guide defines incident roles, escalation, evidence custody, safe rollback, recovery gates, communications and blameless postmortems.

failures.name: No incident commander or shared timeline
failures.symptom: Responders perform conflicting actions and impact estimates differ across channels.
failures.rootCause: The incident is handled as ad-hoc debugging without ownership, roles or a canonical record.
failures.recovery: Declare an incident, appoint a commander, assign technical/security/communications roles and maintain one timestamped timeline.
failures.regressionTest: A simulated incident cannot move to containment until commander and severity are recorded.

failures.name: Containment delayed by investigation
failures.symptom: Data exposure, unsafe tool execution or runaway spend continues while teams gather more detail.
failures.rootCause: Responders prioritize root-cause certainty over stopping active harm.
failures.recovery: Apply the narrowest safe containment first, then continue investigation with preserved evidence.
failures.regressionTest: Active-harm scenario requires a containment action before eradication or recovery.

failures.name: Evidence copied with secrets or overwritten
failures.symptom: Incident ticket contains raw prompts, credentials or customer documents; original logs are lost.
failures.rootCause: Evidence handling lacks redaction, access control, hashing and custody metadata.
failures.recovery: Restrict originals, create redacted derived copies, rotate exposed credentials and record collection/transformation history.
failures.regressionTest: Evidence manifest requires digest, source, collector, timestamp and redaction status.

failures.name: Rollback to unverified artifact
failures.symptom: Service returns but compromised or vulnerable model/image is redeployed.
failures.rootCause: Rollback uses mutable tags or an artifact whose provenance was not checked.
failures.recovery: Select a known-good immutable digest and verify signature/provenance before staged rollout.
failures.regressionTest: Recovery gate rejects unsigned or untrusted rollback artifact.

failures.name: Recovery skips tenant or quality checks
failures.symptom: Service resumes while cross-tenant access, stale cache or model-quality regression remains.
failures.rootCause: Recovery is treated as restarting processes rather than proving system invariants.
failures.recovery: Run security, data integrity, quality/safety, SLO and cost gates before canary and full traffic.
failures.regressionTest: A failed tenant-isolation or quality gate prevents recovery completion.

failures.name: Queue replays harmful work
failures.symptom: Paused jobs execute after restart and repeat unsafe tool calls or data mutations.
failures.rootCause: Queue state, idempotency and authorization are not reviewed before consumers resume.
failures.recovery: Preserve queue evidence, quarantine affected messages, deduplicate and revalidate tenant/actor/resource authorization.
failures.regressionTest: A forged or duplicate job is denied before side effects after recovery.

failures.name: Postmortem actions are not actionable
failures.symptom: The same incident recurs and review notes contain vague actions without completion evidence.
failures.rootCause: Actions lack an owner, due date, priority or verification method.
failures.recovery: Create specific corrective actions with accountable owners, dates and regression/monitoring evidence.
failures.regressionTest: Postmortem cannot be finalized with ownerless or undated actions.

practice.guided: Run the incident simulator for a tenant exposure. Classify severity, select containment, add redacted evidence, attempt recovery with a failed gate, then pass the security/data/quality/SLO gates and complete a postmortem.
practice.independent: Add a model supply-chain compromise scenario. Quarantine the artifact, stop promotion, identify deployments by digest, restore a trusted release, verify provenance and quality, and record customer-impact scope without copying sensitive prompts.
practice.realWorld: Write an incident runbook for a multi-tenant RAG-agent service. Cover tenant exposure, prompt injection with tool exfiltration, compromised model artifacts, provider outage, unsafe tool action and denial-of-wallet. Define roles, severity, containment, evidence, recovery gates and communications.
practice.expertExtension: Run quarterly game days, add automated kill switches, evidence retention/chain-of-custody integration, incident-specific recovery SLOs, customer impact reconciliation, canary recovery gates, and postmortem action aging/escalation.

miniAppIntegration.projectGoal: Build an AI incident-response workbench that classifies severity, guides containment, preserves redacted evidence, validates recovery gates and tracks blameless corrective actions.
steps: Create synthetic incidents for tenant exposure, artifact compromise, provider outage, unsafe tool execution and cost runaway.
Classify severity from impact, exposure, scope and urgency.
Assign commander and response roles and create a canonical timeline.
Apply category-specific containment actions before deep investigation when harm is active.
Collect evidence with digest, source, collector, timestamp, access and redaction metadata.
Run eradication and recovery gates for security, data, model quality, SLO and cost.
Restore a known-good immutable release through a canary and monitor recurrence.
Generate a postmortem with owners, due dates and verification criteria.

scenarioQuiz.question: What is the first priority when active data exfiltration is confirmed?
scenarioQuiz.explanation: Stop ongoing harm with the narrowest effective containment while preserving enough evidence for investigation.

scenarioQuiz.question: What should a rollback target identify?
scenarioQuiz.explanation: An immutable verified digest ensures recovery restores known-good bytes with trusted provenance rather than an artifact that may have changed.

scenarioQuiz.question: What belongs in an evidence custody record?
scenarioQuiz.explanation: Evidence must be attributable and integrity-verifiable; record source, collector, timestamp, digest, access and transformations.

scenarioQuiz.question: When should normal traffic resume?
options: As soon as the process restarts
scenarioQuiz.explanation: Recovery requires security, data-integrity, quality, SLO and operational checks before staged rollout and full traffic.

scenarioQuiz.question: What makes a postmortem action actionable?
scenarioQuiz.explanation: Corrective actions need an accountable owner, deadline and evidence that the control or regression test was completed.

rubric.evidence: Classifies impact and assigns commander, roles and a canonical timeline.
Stops active harm and preserves redacted, integrity-verifiable evidence with custody metadata.
Uses known-good immutable artifacts and passes security, data, quality, SLO and cost gates.
Communicates verified impact and produces a blameless review with owned corrective actions.
Tests incident scenarios, measures response time and adds regression/monitoring evidence.

evidence: Severity and incident commander are recorded before coordinated response.
Active-harm scenarios apply containment before extended investigation.
Evidence includes source, collector, timestamp, digest and redaction status.
Recovery is blocked by any failed security/data/quality/SLO gate.
Rollback uses a verified immutable release digest.
Postmortem actions have owner, due date and verification evidence.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 — Computer Security Incident Handling Guide

codeWalkthrough.explanation: Create one incident record with a canonical timeline and correlation references rather than scattering facts across chat threads.
Classify by user and security impact, not by service status or who reported the issue.
Apply the narrowest effective containment to stop active harm while preserving required evidence.
Preserve integrity-verifiable evidence with source, collector, timestamp, access and transformation metadata.
Select a previously verified release by immutable digest, not a mutable tag or unreviewed branch.
Do not restore normal traffic until required security, data, AI quality, reliability and budget checks pass.
Convert lessons into accountable corrective actions with measurable evidence of completion.
